claims.text: Resistance to simultaneous wear and corrosion in high-entropy alloys is primarily governed by the ability to form and continuously regenerate a fine passivating oxide film.
A self-healing passivating oxide film minimizes exposure of the underlying metal to corrosive agents.
The passivating oxide film reduces friction and mechanical material removal during wear.
An as-cast Fe/Co/Ni/Cr/Mn high-entropy alloy forms a moderate-quality native oxide under ambient conditions.
A small increase in Cr or Al content can promote a more robust and stable nanoscale oxide film.
Controlled oxidation or laser shock peening can promote a more robust and stable nanoscale oxide film.
Moderate mechanical loads permit cyclic abrasion while allowing the oxide film to reform.
Mechanically induced damage to the passive oxide is rapidly healed by spontaneous oxide reformation during tribocorrosion.
Reduced friction caused by the regenerated oxide lowers wear.
The regenerated oxide limits corrosion by preventing direct contact between the underlying metal and electrolyte.
The treated or compositionally modified alloy will have a lower wear rate than the untreated as-cast baseline under matched test conditions.
The treated or compositionally modified alloy will have a lower corrosion current density than the untreated as-cast baseline under matched test conditions.
Continuous healing of the oxide film will significantly reduce combined tribocorrosion degradation.
The untreated as-cast baseline has a native oxide film that forms less effectively under mechanical stress.
The protective effect should hold at moderate loads in electrolytic conditions that provide sufficient time and a suitable environment for oxide regeneration.
Extremely high loads or severe impact can cause the proposed protective mechanism to fail.
Very high temperatures, extremely low pH, or rapidly fluctuating potentials can prevent stable oxide formation and cause the proposed mechanism to fail.
Performance depends on the balance between oxide-film regeneration and removal rates under wear.
The proposed comparison uses an untreated sample and an intervention sample derived from the same high-entropy alloy and tests them under matched tribocorrosion conditions.

Failure to obtain a statistically significant reduction in both wear volume and corrosion current density, or failure to associate improved oxide integrity with degradation resistance, is specified as falsifying the hypothesis.
